target.title: Recurrent Neural Network Transducer for Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
target.venue: 2019 IEEE Automatic Speech Recognition and Understanding Workshop (ASRU 2019)

entries.text: The paper presents a large-scale audio-visual speech recognizer based on an RNN-T.
entries.condition: Authors describe their system and contribution.
entries.quote:
This work presents a large-scale audio-visual speech recog-
nition system based on a recurrent neural network transducer
(RNN-T) architecture.

entries.text: The authors claim a 31k-hour YouTube audio-visual training corpus and a significantly larger dataset than prior systems.
entries.condition: Utterance segments extracted from public YouTube videos; labels come from user-uploaded captions accepted through an ASR agreement pipeline.
entries.quote:
the audio matches
the user-uploaded transcript, and the selected face video track
matches the audio.

entries.text: The authors claim their system significantly improves the state of the art on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: Authors qualify this as best of their knowledge; benchmark results use models trained on YouTube data.
entries.quote:
To the best of our knowledge, our system
signiﬁcantly improves the state-of-the-art on the LRS3-TED
set.

entries.text: They advocate RNN-T as a natural speech model because its recurrent encoder and decoder model local output dependencies and monotonic alignment.
entries.condition: Motivating model-design claim; no separate controlled comparison of these properties is reported.
entries.quote:
We advocate using the recurrent
neural network transducer (RNN-T),

entries.text: Character-level outputs are presented as a simple way to obtain an open-vocabulary system.
entries.condition: RNN-T output symbols are characters; the model's graphemic output space has 75 characters.

entries.text: The authors say the sequence-to-sequence decoder learns a language model implicitly, unlike the external language model they describe as needed by CTC.
entries.condition: Conceptual architecture comparison; evaluation-time external-LM use is not separately specified.

entries.text: The authors propose matching audio feature timing to variable-rate video instead of downsampling the video stream.
entries.condition: The STFT window remains 25 ms while its shift is adjusted to the video frame rate.

entries.text: The source audio corpus mined from YouTube contains about 150k hours before audio-visual filtering.
entries.condition: American English audio-only corpus mined using user-uploaded captions and ASR transcript agreement; it precedes face tracking and audio-visual filtering.

entries.text: Training labels are user-uploaded transcripts retained when ASR transcripts agree after string alignment; face tracking, speaking-face classification, and synchrony filtering then select audio-visual examples.
entries.condition: Automated semi-supervised YouTube mining; user-uploaded captions serve as training reference.

entries.text: The final mined audio-visual corpus totals 31k hours.
entries.condition: Short utterances with high-confidence audio/transcript agreement and a face track judged to match the audio; collected from public YouTube videos.
entries.quote: leading to 31k hours of audio-visual training content.

entries.text: The authors state that their training set is five times larger than the V2P training data and ten times larger than TM-seq2seq training data.
entries.condition: Comparison is by training-data amount: V2P [2] and TM-seq2seq [7].
entries.quote: by a factor of 5

entries.text: The 31k-hour corpus is not augmented by perturbing audio or image data.
entries.condition: Authors identify absence of audio/image perturbation as a limitation of their training set size.

entries.text: The authors state that their training set is ten times larger than the TM-seq2seq training data.
entries.condition: Comparison is by training-data amount against TM-seq2seq [7].

entries.text: A 70-hour development set is extracted to tune the models.
entries.condition: Development data extracted from the automatically constructed training corpus.

entries.text: The YTD EV18 evaluation set contains 20k manually transcribed utterances and totals 25 hours.
entries.condition: Selected from manually transcribed YouTube videos after the same face-tracking process; each retained segment has a matching on-screen speaking face, manual reference transcript, and face track.

entries.text: The YTD EV18 and LRS3-TED evaluation videos are checked against training data by video ID and reported as absent from training.
entries.condition: Video-level exclusion is reported; speaker-level separation is not established.

entries.text: The described LRS3-TED test set contains about 10k words and 1,436 utterances.
entries.condition: Public LRS3-TED test set; the paper's comparison models are trained on other data, and the target RNN-T is trained on YouTube data only.

entries.text: YTD EV18 is synthetically corrupted with NoiseX babble at three SNRs or competing speech at equal energy at an utterance boundary.
entries.condition: Noise is added to YTD EV18 evaluation utterances; babble is randomly selected from NoiseX; overlapping speech is added at the beginning or end.

entries.text: Audio is downmixed to mono at 16 kHz, transformed with an 80-bin log-mel filterbank using a 25 ms window and 10 ms shift, stacked across five frames, then subsampled to one in three frames.
entries.unit: Hz sample rate; filters; ms window; ms shift; stacked frames; fps
entries.condition: Audio front-end for the standard fixed-rate representation; resulting feature dimension is 400.

entries.text: Videos are retained from 23 to 30 fps; face landmarks are temporally smoothed, and 128×128 RGB mouth crops are used after a minimum eye-distance threshold.
entries.unit: fps; pixels minimum eye distance; pixel crop dimensions
entries.condition: High frame rates are downsampled to 30 fps; extreme face pan/tilt angles are not filtered from training examples.

entries.text: For synchronized A/V input, the 25 ms audio analysis window is shifted at one third of the video-frame length, matching audio feature rate to variable video rate.
entries.unit: ms STFT window; video-frame-length fraction per shift
entries.condition: Video frame rates range from 24 to 30 fps in the illustrated synchronization setup.

entries.text: The audio-only RNN-T uses a five-layer bidirectional LSTM encoder with 512 nodes in each direction, a two-layer unidirectional LSTM decoder projected to 640, a 640-dimensional joint space, and a 75-character output space.
entries.unit: encoder layers; nodes per direction; decoder layers; joint dimensions; output characters
entries.condition: Audio-only RNN-T architecture; input consists of 400-dimensional stacked filterbank features.

entries.text: The visual frontend has five 3×3×3 convolution blocks, group normalization with 32 groups, a 512-dimensional per-frame embedding, and 11.7M parameters.
entries.unit: blocks; normalization groups; embedding coefficients; parameters
entries.condition: Video model described as using the V2P feature architecture; group normalization is over spatial, not temporal, dimensions.

entries.text: The A/V system concatenates the 400-dimensional audio and 512-dimensional visual features; the full model has 62.9M parameters.
entries.unit: audio dimensions; visual dimensions; concatenated dimensions; parameters
entries.condition: Joint A/V model architecture; parameter total excludes temporary training-only variables such as moment estimates.

entries.text: Training uses Adam with a learning rate warming to 2×10⁻³ over 20k steps, held constant for 50k steps, then exponentially decayed unless noted otherwise.
entries.unit: learning rate; warm-up steps; constant-rate steps
entries.condition: Default schedule; the dual-modality-dropout model uses a separately reported schedule.

entries.text: Training uses 128 TPU cores and 16 examples per core, giving a stated effective batch size of 2,048 utterances per step.
entries.unit: TPU cores; utterances per core; utterances per step
entries.condition: Training setup for reported models.

entries.text: The selected checkpoint is the one with the best result on a held-out validation shard of training data.
entries.condition: 70 hours are also described as a development set for tuning; the relationship between that set and the validation shard is not specified.

entries.text: WER is measured from a frame-synchronized beam decoder retaining at most four highest-scoring candidates at each decoding step; intervals are reported as half-width 95% confidence intervals.
entries.condition: The paper attributes confidence-interval computation to reference [31].

entries.text: Audio-only RNN-T obtains 21.5% WER on YTD EV18.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; audio-only training and evaluation; 31k-hour YouTube training corpus; frame-synchronized beam decoder with beam width at most 4.

entries.text: Visual-only RNN-T obtains 48.5% WER on YTD EV18.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; visual-only training and evaluation; 31k-hour YouTube training corpus; frame-synchronized beam decoder with beam width at most 4.

entries.text: Audio-visual RNN-T obtains 20.5% WER on YTD EV18.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; audio-visual training and evaluation; 31k-hour YouTube training corpus; frame-synchronized beam decoder with beam width at most 4.

entries.text: The authors report that A/V RNN-T can be trained from scratch without pretraining any component.
entries.condition: Training on the 31k-hour audio-visual corpus; result table compares audio, visual, and combined modes.

entries.text: With no modality dropout, an A/V-trained model scores 24.0% on audio-only, 98.8% on visual-only, and 20.5% on A/V YTD EV18 inputs.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; model trained A+V without modality dropout; tested in audio-only, visual-only, and A+V modes, respectively.

entries.text: With 30% audio dropout, the A/V-trained model scores 46.0% on audio-only, 50.3% on visual-only, and 19.8% on A/V YTD EV18 inputs.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; A/V model trained with 30% sentence-level audio dropout and no visual dropout; tested in audio-only, visual-only, and A+V modes, respectively.

entries.text: With 30% audio dropout and 10% video dropout, the model scores 45.6% on audio-only, 55.3% on visual-only, and 20.0% on A/V YTD EV18 inputs.
entries.condition: YTD EV18; A/V model trained with sentence-level dropout of audio and video; tested in audio-only, visual-only, and A+V modes, respectively.

entries.text: Audio dropout makes the model nearly as effective as the unimodal visual model, while substantially worsening audio-only evaluation; the authors conclude concatenation fusion is not robust across missing modalities.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation of YTD EV18 results under sentence-level modality dropout.
entries.quote:
They also indicate that the current strategy of modality fusion
through the concatenation of features is not robust to these
different input conditions.

entries.text: The model with both audio and video dropout uses a learning rate of 4×10⁻³ held constant until 100k steps.
entries.condition: A/V training with 30% audio dropout and 10% video dropout; schedule changed to compensate for slower learning.

entries.text: Visual-only training and testing at variable, 33⅓, 30, and 24 fps produce 48.5%, 48.6%, 48.5%, and 50.1% WER, respectively.
entries.unit: % WER (95% CI ±0.6 for each); fps settings variable, 33⅓, 30, 24
entries.condition: YTD EV18; visual-only training and evaluation; each setting uses the named frame rate for both train and test.

entries.text: A/V training and evaluation at variable, 33⅓, 30, and 24 fps produce 19.8%, 20.4%, 20.2%, and 20.1% WER, respectively.
entries.unit: % WER (95% CI ±0.5 for each); fps settings variable, 33⅓, 30, 24
entries.condition: YTD EV18; A+V training and evaluation; each setting uses the named frame rate for both train and test; default 30% audio dropout used for reported later experiments.

entries.text: Audio-only training and evaluation at variable, 33⅓, 30, and 24 fps produce 21.5%, 21.6%, 21.2%, and 21.4% WER, respectively.
entries.unit: % WER (95% CI ±0.5 for each); fps settings variable, 33⅓, 30, 24
entries.condition: YTD EV18; audio-only training and evaluation; each setting uses the named frame rate for both train and test.

entries.text: The authors conclude variable-rate input is as effective as fixed frame rates for RNN-T in their experiment.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 frame-rate comparison; authors note a different learning-rate schedule produced slightly better fixed-30-fps accuracy.
entries.quote:
We can conclude, using
a variable frame rate is as effective as using ﬁxed frame rates
with an RNN-T model.

entries.text: For uncorrupted YTD EV18, audio-only and A/V models score 21.5% and 20.5% WER; visual-only is reported as 48.5% across noise conditions.
entries.condition: Models trained on uncorrupted data; YTD EV18 clean evaluation; visual-only score is the noise-invariant value reported in the table/text.

entries.text: With babble at 20 dB, uncorrupted-training audio-only and A/V systems score 22.5% and 21.2% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble added at 20 dB SNR; audio and A/V models trained on uncorrupted data.

entries.text: With babble at 10 dB, uncorrupted-training audio-only, A/V, and visual-only systems score 28.1%, 24.8%, and 48.5% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble added at 10 dB SNR; audio, A/V, and visual systems trained on uncorrupted data.

entries.text: With babble at 0 dB, uncorrupted-training audio-only and A/V systems score 64.5% and 57.4% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble added at 0 dB SNR; audio and A/V models trained on uncorrupted data; visual-only results are reported as 48.5% across added-noise conditions in the accompanying text.

entries.text: With overlapping speech, uncorrupted-training audio-only and A/V systems score 40.6% and 37.4% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with equal-energy competing speech added at the beginning or end; audio and A/V models trained on uncorrupted data.
entries.quote: overlapping speech 40.6±0.6 37.4±0.6

entries.text: The authors report that the A/V advantage over audio-only grows in noisier test conditions, and visual-only is best under severe babble.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 corrupted evaluation; no added noise in the audio training data for these Table 5 models.

entries.text: Overlap augmentation is applied with 10% probability, mixing a randomly selected training utterance at a level uniformly selected from 0–20 dB.
entries.condition: Training audio augmentation for Table 6 models; utterance is randomly selected from the training set.
entries.quote:
with a 10% chance at a level between 0-20dB randomly
selected over a uniform distribution.

entries.text: With overlap-augmented training, clean YTD EV18 audio-only and A/V systems score 21.0% and 20.0% WER; visual-only is reported as 48.5% across conditions.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 without added test noise; audio and A/V models trained with 10% overlap augmentation; visual-only value is reported as invariant across conditions.

entries.text: With babble at 20 dB and overlap-augmented training, audio-only and A/V systems score 21.9% and 20.5% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble at 20 dB SNR; training audio augmented with 10% overlap mixtures.

entries.text: With babble at 10 dB and overlap-augmented training, audio-only, A/V, and visual-only systems score 26.6%, 23.1%, and 48.5% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble at 10 dB SNR; audio, A/V, and visual models trained with 10% overlap augmentation.

entries.text: With babble at 0 dB and overlap-augmented training, audio-only and A/V systems score 57.7% and 42.3% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with NoiseX babble at 0 dB SNR; audio and A/V models trained with 10% overlap augmentation; visual-only value reported as invariant across conditions.

entries.text: With overlapping-speech test audio and overlap-augmented training, audio-only and A/V systems score 31.5% and 25.6% WER.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 with equal-energy competing speech added at an utterance boundary; training audio augmented with 10% overlap mixtures.
entries.quote: overlapping speech 31.5±0.6 25.6±0.6

entries.text: The authors attribute larger relative gains under 0 dB babble and overlapping speech to visual input and hypothesize that it helps ignore competing speech.
entries.condition: Authors' interpretation of Table 6, with overlap added to training audio at 10% probability.

entries.text: Prior visual-only TM-seq2seq result on LRS3-TED is 58.9% WER.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; TM-seq2seq trained on 1.4k hours of BBC+TED data; prior published result.

entries.text: Prior audio-only TM-seq2seq result on LRS3-TED is 8.3% WER.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; TM-seq2seq trained on 1.4k hours of BBC+TED data; prior published result.

entries.text: Prior audio-visual TM-seq2seq result on LRS3-TED is 7.2% WER.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; TM-seq2seq trained on 1.4k hours of BBC+TED data; prior published result.
entries.quote: BBC+TED, 1.4khrs TM-seq2seq A+V 7.2

entries.text: YouTube-trained visual-only RNN-T obtains 33.6% WER on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; visual-only RNN-T trained on 31k hours of YouTube data, with no LRS3-TED training data; beam decoder as described in Sec. 4.
entries.quote: YT, 31khrs RNN-T V 33.6

entries.text: YouTube-trained audio-only RNN-T obtains 4.8% WER on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; audio-only RNN-T trained on 31k hours of YouTube data; no external LRS3-TED training data is used.

entries.text: YouTube-trained audio-visual RNN-T obtains 4.5% WER on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS3-TED; audio-visual RNN-T trained on 31k hours of YouTube data; no LRS3-TED training data is used.
entries.quote: YT, 31khrs RNN-T A+V 4.5

entries.text: The authors say the LRS3-TED results improve on both cited visual-speech systems and that A/V improves over audio-only on this test set.
entries.condition: Comparison uses 31k hours of YouTube training for RNN-T, 4k hours for CTC-V2P, and 1.4k hours of BBC+TED for TM-seq2seq.

entries.text: On YTD EV18, visual-only WER is 57.0% for low-quality utterances and 37.1% for high-quality utterances; 70% of utterances are categorized as low quality.
entries.condition: Quality labels use minimum eye distance 80 pixels, bounding-box diagonal 300 pixels, maximum absolute pan angle 30 degrees, and tilt angle below 10 degrees for high quality; remaining utterances are low quality.

entries.text: The authors attribute the lower LRS3-TED visual-only WER partly to professionally produced video, good lighting, at least 24 fps, and a cooperative frontal speaker; YTD EV18 is more in-the-wild.
entries.unit: fps minimum stated for LRS3-TED conditions
entries.condition: Authors contrast 33.6% visual-only WER on LRS3-TED with 48.5% on YTD EV18.

entries.text: The authors expect further performance degradation on low-resolution, low-frame-rate video such as CCTV.
entries.condition: Authors' expectation; no CCTV evaluation is reported.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge privacy risks and state that project data and models are restricted to a small group of researchers and handled under GDPR.
entries.condition: No public release of the mined training data or trained models is stated.
entries.quote:
the data and models devel-
oped in this work are restricted to a small group of researchers

entries.text: The authors identify comparisons with attention-based and transformer-based models and modality-imbalanced training as future work.
entries.condition: These comparisons are not reported in this paper.
entries.quote:
Future
work will focus on comparing the performance of our sys-
tem with other alternative approaches

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds, number of independent training runs, or across-run variability.
entries.condition: Applies to model training and reported evaluation results; confidence intervals are described for WER, but no seed or repeat protocol is given.
entries.quote:
For all results, we
select the model checkpoint that produces the best result on
a held-out validation shard of the training data.

entries.text: Speaker-level train/test disjointness is not reported; only video-ID exclusion is described.
entries.condition: The paper confirms evaluation videos are absent from training, but does not state whether any speakers recur across training and evaluation.

entries.text: The paper does not report the number or identities of speakers in YTD EV18 or LRS3-TED evaluation, nor speaker-stratified results.
entries.condition: Evaluation-set composition; video-level exclusion is reported but speaker statistics are not.

entries.text: The precise LRS3-TED evaluation partition or split identifier is not given beyond calling it the test set.
entries.condition: The paper reports about 10k words and 1,436 utterances but does not name a specific LRS3-TED split/version.

entries.text: The paper does not specify WER text normalization, including case, punctuation, tokenization, or treatment of disfluencies and numbers.
entries.condition: Applies to YTD EV18, noisy YTD EV18, and LRS3-TED scoring.

entries.text: No chance-level or chance-baseline performance is reported for the recognition task.
entries.condition: Reported comparisons are model WERs and prior-system WERs; no chance baseline is described.

entries.text: The exact construction, size, and separation from the 70-hour development set of the held-out validation shard are not specified; the validation selection metric is not named.
entries.condition: Checkpoint selection uses a held-out shard of training data; a separate 70-hour development set is mentioned for tuning.

entries.text: The evaluation description does not state whether an external language model or lexicon is used, or give any LM weight or fusion settings.
entries.condition: RNN-T is described as learning a language model in its decoder; only beam candidate count is specified for evaluation decoding.
entries.quote:
In contrast, using a sequence-to-
sequence loss allows the language model to be learned implic-
itly as part of the decoder.

entries.text: Exact durations, overlap-speaker selection, mixing implementation, and random seeds for evaluation-time competing-speech corruption are not stated.
entries.condition: Paper says a few seconds of competing speech are added at the beginning or end at equal energy, but does not give exact durations or selection details.

entries.text: Noise utterance identities, random seeds, and exact noise mixing/normalization procedure are not reported for the babble test conditions.
entries.condition: NoiseX babble is randomly selected and added at named SNRs; details of the random selection and implementation are absent.

entries.text: The exact test-set selection threshold for a face track covering 'most' of the speech and being 'well synchronized' is not quantified.
entries.condition: The selected YTDEV18 evaluation subset is described qualitatively; the paper reports no numerical coverage or synchrony criterion for that subset.

entries.text: The paper reports 95% confidence-interval half-widths but does not give the evaluation sample unit or a resampling/repetition procedure in the paper text.
entries.condition: Confidence intervals are attributed to a cited WER method; the text does not detail the sampling unit or evaluation repetitions.

entries.text: Seventy percent of YTD EV18 utterances are labeled low quality under the authors' face-size and pose criteria.
entries.condition: High quality requires minimum eye distance 80 pixels, bounding-box diagonal 300 pixels, maximum absolute pan 30 degrees, and tilt below 10 degrees; other utterances are low quality.

entries.text: The YTD EV18 evaluation-selection pool begins with 1,000 hours of manually transcribed YouTube videos.
entries.condition: Manually transcribed YouTube source pool, filtered using the training face-tracking process to retain utterances with a matching on-screen face.

entries.text: The selected YTDEV18 evaluation utterances are collected from over 1,000 videos.
entries.condition: Selection requires visual tracks covering most of the speech and being well synchronized; the paper does not quantify the threshold.

entries.text: No explicit mean/variance, cepstral, or other acoustic feature normalization procedure is specified beyond log-mel filterbank extraction and LSTM layer normalization.
entries.condition: Input representation normalization for training and evaluation is not detailed; layer normalization is separately stated for the LSTM layers.

entries.text: The authors report that adding video dropout harmed visual-only results by 10% relative, so later results use audio dropout without video dropout.
entries.condition: A/V model trained with 30% audio dropout and 10% video dropout; visual-only YTD EV18 evaluation.

entries.text: Frame-rate differences are described as not significant, although a fixed 30-fps model was slightly better under a different learning-rate schedule.
entries.condition: YTD EV18 comparison between variable and fixed frame-rate models; the stated slight advantage was observed with a different learning-rate schedule.

entries.text: The paper compares CTC loss with sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) loss.
Video is sampled at 25 fps; each video frame corresponds to four acoustic feature frames.
entries.quote:
Since the video is sampled at 25 fps (40
ms per frame), every video input frame corresponds to 4 acoustic
feature frames.

entries.text: Training adds babble noise at 0dB SNR with probability 0.25.
entries.loc: 5.3 Training with noisy audio & multi-modal training

entries.text: The LRS3-TED pre-train set contains 444 hours.
The LRS3-TED train-val set contains 30 hours.
The LSVSR dataset contains 3,886 hours of audio-video-text pairs.
entries.quote:
In comparison,
our dataset (LSVSR) is an order of magnitude greater than any previous dataset with 3,886 hours of
audio-video-text pairs.

entries.text: The pipeline builds on Liao et al. (2013) to extract transcript-paired audio clips, yielding 140,000 hours of audio segments.
entries.quote:
In our case, we build on the work of Liao et al. (2013) to extract audio clips paired with transcripts,
yielding 140,000 hours of audio segments.
entries.loc: 3 A DATA PIPELINE FOR LARGE-SCALE VISUAL SPEECH RECOGNITION

entries.text: The model is trained using CTC loss.
entries.quote:
Given input video clips and
target phoneme sequences the model is trained using the CTC loss function.
entries.loc: 4 AN EFFICIENT SPATIOTEMPORAL MODEL OF VISUAL SPEECH RECOGNITION

entries.text: At test time, an FST-based decoder produces word sequences.
entries.quote:
Finally, at test-time, a
decoder based on ﬁnite state transducers (FSTs) is used to produce a word sequence given a sequence
of phoneme distributions.
entries.loc: 4 AN EFFICIENT SPATIOTEMPORAL MODEL OF VISUAL SPEECH RECOGNITION

entries.text: The described Seq2seq architecture is attention-based, with an encoder, decoder, and attender.
entries.quote:
The attention based Seq2seq architecture [8] consists of a s equence
encoder, a sequence decoder and an attender.

entries.text: The three approaches listed are CTC, RNN-T, and attention-based encoder-decoder.
entries.quote:
Connectionist temporal classiﬁcation (CTC) [3, 4], RNN tra nsducer
(RNN-T) [5, 6, 7] and attention based encoder-decoder [8, 9, 10] are
the three main approaches.

entries.text: The reported visual features are upsampled to 50 fps by linear interpolation.
entries.quote:
It should be noted that the results shown cor-
respond to visual features upsampled to 50 fps using linear
interpolation.

entries.text: The paper uses a hybrid CTC/attention architecture for audio-visual speech recognition.
entries.quote:
In this paper, we use the recently
proposed hybrid CTC/attention architecture for audio-visual
recognition of speech in-the-wild.

entries.text: The VSR decoder is RNN-T, implemented as a 9-layer LSTM with cell size 2048, embedding dimension 128, and beam width 8.
entries.unit: LSTM layers; cell size; embedding; beam width
entries.quote:
For the decoder, we use RNN-T, a
9-layer LSTM with cell size 2048, embedding dimension 128, and
beam width 8.

entries.text: The model reports 12.8% WER on the TED LRS3 benchmark.
entries.condition: TED LRS3 visual-only; trained on YT 100k h then fine-tuned on TED-LRS3; RNN-T decoder
entries.quote:
The proposed one-patch model performs extremely well, achiev-
ing a new state-of-the-art word error rate of 12.8% on the widely
used TED LRS3 benchmark.

entries.text: The LP Conformer reports 0.9% audio-visual WER on TED-LRS3.
entries.condition: TED-LRS3 audio-visual, LP Conformer, RNN-T decoder, YT 100k h
entries.quote:
The LP Conformer obtains state-of-the-art
results on A VSR for TED-LRS3, achieving0.9% WER when trained
and tested on the full audio-visual input (c.f. Table 2).

entries.text: The YouTube dataset contains 100,000 hours of transcribed video segments.
entries.quote:
The YT
dataset contains 100k hours of transcribed video segments that are
up to 15 seconds long.

entries.text: Whisper-Flamingo reports state-of-the-art 0.76% AVSR WER on LRS3.
entries.condition: LRS3 / LRS2 ASR and AVSR; Whisper-initialised; attention decoder
entries.quote:
Our models achieve state-of-the-art ASR
WER (0.68%) and A VSR WER (0.76%) on LRS3, and state-
of-the-art ASR WER (1.3%) and A VSR WER (1.4%) on LRS2.

entries.text: Whisper uses a Transformer attention decoder with self-attention and cross-attention to audio features.
entries.quote:
Each of Whisper’s decoder blocks consists of a
self-attention layer, cross attention layer attending to the au-
dio features, and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP).

entries.text: Makino et al.’s online audio-visual model is based on RNN-T and uses direct feature fusion.
entries.condition: [later] work, first public 2020-12

entries.text: Makino et al. tailor audio feature extraction to the video frame rate using variable increments to the spectral analysis window.
entries.condition: [later] work, first public 2020-12

entries.text: AV Taris uses a seq2seq backend, avoiding RNN-T-specific training difficulties.
entries.condition: [later] work, first public 2020-12

entries.text: Sentence-level modality dropout is adopted as in the authors' reference [32] (Zhang et al., ICASSP 2019, bimodal DFSMN with dropout regularization).
entries.condition: Sec. 4.2; [32] is not in the wiki
entries.quote: we simulate the effect during training by randomly dropping out a modality at the sentence level as in [32]

questions.q: What evidence supports the paper's state-of-the-art claim, and what limits a direct comparison?
questions.answer: On LRS3-TED, the paper reports its YouTube-trained RNN-T results alongside CTC-V2P and TM-seq2seq results and claims improvement over both. Training corpora differ in source and size, and the paper does not provide detailed split or scoring-normalization information for the comparisons.

questions.q: How does missing or noisy audio affect the visual contribution?
questions.answer: Without modality dropout, the A/V-trained model performs poorly on visual-only input; sentence-level audio dropout substantially improves visual-only robustness. Under severe babble and overlapping speech, the reported A/V WER is lower than audio-only, with further gains after overlap augmentation.

questions.q: Which evaluation and reproducibility conditions remain unspecified?
questions.answer: The paper does not report training seeds or repeat counts, speaker-level separation, exact WER normalization, a chance baseline, detailed noise-generation randomness, or full validation-shard construction and selection criteria. It confirms only video-ID-level exclusion between evaluation videos and training data.

questions.q: Is the dataset or model available for independent evaluation?
questions.answer: The paper states that its data and models are restricted to a small group of project researchers; it provides no public code link.

questions.q: Does variable frame rate outperform fixed-rate audio-video input?
questions.answer: The authors describe the differences as not significant and conclude that variable frame rate is as effective as fixed rates; a fixed 30-fps model was slightly better only under a different learning-rate schedule.
